**Before the visit**
- Add the appointment date in the Visit tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and how to make them fuller.
- Pick the topics and questions that matter most to you, keeping to three or four.
- Generate notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the visit**
- Hand the first page to the doctor, or show it to them. This page is designed to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor uses another language, you can generate the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

The notes summarize what you logged and what you chose to import from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis and not a complete medical record; any patterns in them are only a coincidence check and cannot prove cause and effect. The doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the visit**

Add any new medication and its start date. After a few weeks, MenoMap can show your records from before and after you started it, making the next follow-up easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a point in time: the day after 12 consecutive months without a period, which cannot be explained by other causes (such as pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but anywhere from about 45 to about 55 is common.

**Perimenopause** is the several years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unpredictably, so periods may become irregular, heavier or lighter, closer together or further apart. Many changes people associate with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin at this stage, while periods are still happening. Perimenopause may last a few years or much longer, and it differs for each person.

**Postmenopause** is all the time after the 12 months are complete. Some symptoms ease over time, while others may last for years.

Menopause can also occur early because of surgery removing the ovaries, certain cancer treatments, or other health problems. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency and is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How to tell.** For many people over 45, the doctor judges from your history and symptoms whether you are in perimenopause or have reached menopause. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels fluctuate daily. Blood tests are more likely to be needed when you are younger or the situation is unclear.

**What MenoMap can and cannot do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is faithfully record what you notice: hot flashes, sleep, mood and treatments, so that you and your doctor see the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with skin flushing, sweating, a racing heart, or feeling chilled afterward. Night sweats are the same thing occurring during sleep, and can be intense enough to wake you or soak the sheets.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have only a few mild ones; some have several a day, affecting work and sleep. In some people they fade within a few years; in others they last longer.

**What may make them more likely.** People often find they are linked to alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, stuffy rooms, stress or heavy bedding. These vary a lot from person to person, so recording your own tags may be more useful than a generic list.

**There can also be other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also come from thyroid problems, infection, certain medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the common pattern, or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell your doctor.

**How to describe it more clearly.** Useful details at the visit:
- Roughly how many during the day and at night
- How intense they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversation, exercise
- What seemed to come before them
- What you have tried and whether it made a difference

MenoMap's hot flash button and after-the-fact logging feature exist precisely to record this information without effort.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, and also some practical approaches. Which suit you needs to be discussed with your doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) is used to replace part of the estrogen the body makes less of around menopause. Major guidelines consider it, for many people, an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats, and it may also help relieve other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as vaginal dryness. For people who still have a uterus, doctors usually prescribe a progestogen in addition to estrogen, to protect the uterine lining.

**Benefits and risks vary by person:** depending on age, how long since periods stopped, personal and family medical history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and the type and route of treatment. So this is a decision to make with a doctor who knows your history, not one an app can make for you.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy right for me? Why or why not?
- Which type and form would you recommend? Why?
- What benefits can I expect, and how soon?
- What are my personal risks? How do they compare with no treatment?
- What should I watch for? When should I have a follow-up?

**If you are already using it,** record it in MenoMap (Me -> Medications). MenoMap will show your hot flashes before and after you started, as a coincidence check, not evidence, so you have something concrete to discuss at your follow-up.

MenoMap never recommends starting, stopping or changing any medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not right for everyone, and some people simply prefer other routes. There are several other routes.

**Prescription medications.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence of reducing hot flashes. These include some drugs originally developed for other conditions, and a newer class developed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, and a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking and mind-body therapies.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence of reducing the distress caused by hot flashes and night sweats, and improving sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes people find helpful:**
- Wear layers that can be taken off quickly
- Keep a fan at the desk and by the bed
- Make the bedroom cooler and use breathable bedding
- Notice and reduce personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments can help)
- Be active regularly and keep a steady sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal products.** For many of these the evidence is mixed or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about any products you take, including over-the-counter ones.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiment compares your records before and during the change, which is easier to judge than going by feel.

backTranslations.416:
Most visits are short, and it is hard to recall a month of nights on the spot. People tend to remember only the last few days or the worst days. A simple log can fill that gap.

**What a diary can give the doctor:**
- How often and how intense symptoms are, not just "has symptoms"
- Whether things are getting better, worse or staying the same
- What was happening around them: sleep, drinking, stress, medications
- If you try a treatment, a starting point to compare against

**Keep it easy.** A diary is only useful if you keep at it. MenoMap is built around a one-tap hot flash button and a four-question evening check-in, which takes a few seconds, no notebook needed.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of records usually shows the whole picture better than a single bad week on its own.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptoms bothering you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Visit tab can help you pick questions and print them together with the notes.

backTranslations.479:
Once you have gone 12 consecutive months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a doctor**, even if it happened only once, even if it is only spotting, or light pink or brown discharge.

Most of the time the cause is not serious, for example thinning of the vagina or uterine lining is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is easier to treat the earlier it is found. So public health guidelines recommend getting it checked rather than waiting.

**If you are using hormone therapy,** depending on the type you use, some bleeding patterns may be expected. Bleeding that is not expected for your treatment, bleeding heavier than usual, or bleeding at a time when it should not occur should also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or healthcare provider and tell them you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount of bleeding and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can help you keep this information (Me -> Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you the cause of the bleeding. It will remind you to get it checked and write it into your visit notes.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common troubles of midlife, and it rarely has just one cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or leave you too hot and damp to fall asleep again.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to get up at night to urinate
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol: it may help you fall asleep, but often makes the second half of the night fragmented
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs, or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or breathing pauses, which may be a sign of sleep apnea (worth raising, especially with heavy daytime sleepiness)

**What usually helps people.** A cool dark room; breathable bedding and layers you can take off at any time; a fixed wake-up time; and drinking less before bed. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-researched approach that many doctors can refer you to.

**What to record.** Over a week or two, note your sleep score, night hot flashes, drinking and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check-in and hot flash logging take just a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside your night sweats, as background reference, not explanation.

**When to see a doctor.** If poor sleep affects your safety (for example driving), mood or daily life, or you notice breathing pauses or gasping at night, talk to a doctor.
